title: Meditation: Resting the Mind at Ease
author: Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche
excerpt: Excerpted from Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche, Ground, Path, and Fruition: The Methods and Stages of Meditation

inline.s: Excerpted from Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche, Ground, Path, and Fruition: The Methods and Stages of Meditation
We must go through this process — that is, truly sitting down to examine our own mind,
examining our own experience — for only then can we see clearly what is really going on.
— Kalu Rinpoche, The Precious Treasury of Oral Instructions
To realize the meaning of mind is to realize everything.
Jamgön
Kongtrül
Lodrö Thaye, The Outline of Essential Points

First of all, I want to confess something to you all. Ever since childhood, fear and anxiety have plagued me without letup. Whenever I found myself among strangers, my heart would race and cold sweat would pour down my back. That this should happen to a reincarnate lama seems very strange, for has not such a one accumulated vast roots of virtue and meritorious deeds over many lifetimes? The unease I felt then had no reason to it at all. I was living in a beautiful valley, surrounded by loving family, by monks and nuns, and by people devoted to learning how to awaken inner peace and joy. And yet anxiety was my constant companion.

I learned that Sherab Ling was about to hold a traditional three-year retreat, and that the retreat master would be Saljay Rinpoche. Saljay Rinpoche was recognized throughout the Tibetan Buddhist world as one of the most accomplished masters of the older generation, and he was one of my principal teachers at Sherab Ling. Gentle and kind, with a deep, low voice, he had an uncanny ability to say or do exactly the right thing at exactly the right time. I am sure you too have met people like this — people who somehow teach you extraordinarily profound dharma without your even noticing it, and whose very bearing is a lesson that serves you for the rest of your life.
Because Saljay Rinpoche was already advanced in years, this might well be the last retreat he would ever guide, and so I truly wanted to take part. But at that time I was only

years old, and it was generally thought that this was far too young to endure the rigors of a three-year retreat. I begged my father to intercede for me, and in the end Tai Situ Rinpoche gave me permission to join the retreat.

I wish I could tell you that everything began to improve once I arrived at Sherab Ling, settled in, and joined the other three-year retreatants. But the truth was exactly the opposite: the first year of retreat was the most miserable year of my life. Every anxiety symptom I had ever experienced — tension in the body, a constricted throat, dizziness, and waves of panic that were especially intense during group practice — descended on me all at once. In Western terms, I had a nervous breakdown.

What I would say now is that what I went through should really be called a “spiritual breakthrough.” During the retreat, entirely free of the distractions of daily life, I found myself in a situation where I had to face my own mind directly. And my mind was not exactly pleased, day after day, with the scenery it beheld; as each week passed, the landscape of my mind and emotions seemed to grow more and more terrifying. Toward the end of that first year of retreat, I finally realized that I had to make a choice: over the next two years, would I go on hiding in my room, or would I truly accept the truth my father and my other teachers had taught me — that whatever problems I was experiencing were nothing but habits of thought and perception rooted in my own mind?

I decided to follow their teachings. For three days I stayed in my room, meditating with many of the techniques that will be described later in this book. Gradually I began to recognize that the thoughts and emotions that had plagued me for years were actually fragile and fleeting, and to see how clinging to small problems turns them into big ones. I simply sat quietly, watching how thoughts and emotions come and go so swiftly and so often illogically. I began to know “directly” that thoughts and emotions are not as solid or as real as they appear. Once I stopped believing the stories they told me, I began to see the “author” behind them — the boundless, utterly open awareness that is the nature of mind.

Trying to capture in words the direct experience of the nature of mind is simply impossible. At most we can say that this experience is utterly peaceful, and that once it has been repeated until it gradually grows stable, it becomes almost unshakable. It is an experience of absolute well-being that radiates through every physical, emotional, and mental state — even through states that we would ordinarily consider unpleasant. This sense of well-being is unaffected by changes in outer or inner experience, and it is one of the clearest ways of understanding what Buddhists mean by “happiness.” I was very fortunate to catch a glimpse of it during those three days alone.

Three days later I came out of my room and rejoined the group practice. After two more weeks of single-minded meditation, I finally overcame the anxiety that had shadowed me since childhood, and through direct experience I understood the truth my teachers had taught. From that time on, my panic attacks never recurred. And the peace, confidence, and well-being born of that experience have never wavered, even in situations generally regarded as highly stressful. The transformation I went through was not my own doing; I merely applied with diligence the truth handed down by those who came before me.
When I came out of retreat I was

years old, and to my surprise Tai Situ Rinpoche appointed me retreat master for the next retreat, which was soon to begin. Within a few months I was back in the retreat hut, teaching the preliminary and the more advanced practices of the Kagyu lineage and guiding the new retreatants into the very same stream of transmission that I had received directly. Although I was the retreat master, for me this was in fact a most precious opportunity to practice intensively in retreat for nearly
years. This time, I was no longer hiding in my little room in fear and dread.
Whatever arises, simply look at its nature.
Karma
Chagme Rinpoche, The Union of Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen

The Buddha understood that no two people in this world are exactly alike, and that each person’s innate abilities, traits, and temperament differ. Out of his great insight and compassion, the Buddha developed countless skillful means, so that all beings, through these various methods, might have the chance to realize directly their own true nature and thereby be completely freed from suffering.

Most of the Buddha’s teachings were given spontaneously, in response to the needs of the people around him at the time. This ability to respond precisely to the needs of beings in the moment is in fact one of the marks of a realized master. As long as a realized master is alive, there is no problem in transmitting instruction and resolving doubts. After the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, however, his senior disciples — so that his teachings might go on benefiting later generations — had to devise a method for systematically organizing these spontaneously given instructions. Fortunately, the Buddha’s senior disciples were extremely skilled at classification, and they divided the various meditation methods the Buddha had taught into two broad categories: analytic meditation and nonanalytic meditation.

In the study of meditation, nonanalytic meditation is usually taught first, because this practice provides a way to settle the mind; once the mind is settled, it becomes easier to notice thoughts, emotions, and sense perceptions without being caught up in them. Analytic meditation, by contrast, means looking directly at the mind within various experiences, and it is usually taught only after students have learned to rest the mind as it is. Moreover, because the practice of looking at the mind easily gives rise to many questions, analytic meditation is best done under the guidance of a teacher who has both insight and practical experience, since such a teacher can understand a student’s questions deeply and offer answers tailored to that student. So the focus I want to discuss here is the method of settling and pacifying the mind — that is, nonanalytic meditation.

In Sanskrit, nonanalytic meditation is called śamatha, which means “calm abiding,” or “the meditation of calm abiding”; in Tibetan it is shiné. The word has two syllables: shi means peace or tranquility, and né means to dwell or remain. The full translation of this practice, then, is “peacefully dwelling,” that is, allowing the mind to dwell peacefully just as it is. This is a basic practice through which we naturally rest the mind in relaxed awareness, so that the nature of mind reveals itself.
Go straight to the root of mind: rest in naked awareness.
— Tilopa, The Ganges Mahāmudrā
When my father first taught me to let the mind rest naturally “in naked awareness,” I had no idea what he was talking about. If there is no place to rest, how am I supposed to “rest” the mind on it?

Fortunately, by then my father had traveled to many countries, met many people, and talked with them about their lives, their difficulties, their accomplishments, and so on. This is indeed one of the advantages of wearing monastic robes: people generally assume you are wise or important, and so they are willing to open their hearts and tell you the ins and outs of their lives.
To explain how to rest the mind, my father told the story of a hotel clerk who had to stand behind the counter

hours a day, checking guests in and out, listening to their complaints about the rooms, and often arguing with them over the bill. So whenever his shift was about to end, he was always overjoyed. After a whole day’s work he was exhausted, and he looked forward to going home, soaking in a hot bath, and then lying down on his bed, letting out a deep sigh, and relaxing completely. The next few hours belonged to him alone: he did not have to stand there in uniform, did not have to listen to anyone complain, and did not have to stare at a computer screen confirming bookings and checking whether any rooms were still free.

This is what resting the mind in objectless calm-abiding meditation is like: it is like having just finished a long, hard day’s work — all you have to do is let go and relax. You do not need to stop any thought, emotion, or sense perception from arising, and you do not need to follow them either; simply rest in the open present, letting them happen. If a thought or emotion arises, just let yourself clearly notice that it is there. Objectless calm-abiding meditation does not mean letting your mind wander aimlessly through fantasies, memories, or daydreams. In meditation you may not be focusing on any particular object, but you are still aware, still clearly cognizant of everything happening in the present. This is a certain manifestation of the mind itself, which we can sum up as a center of awareness.

When we meditate in the objectless state, we are in fact resting the mind in its own innate clarity, utterly without attachment to the coming and going of any thought or emotion. This natural clarity, which transcends self and other, is always with us, just as space is always present right here and now. We might say that objectless meditation is like accepting the clouds and mist that drift across the sky from time to time, while knowing clearly that the sky itself remains unchanging even when it is obscured. If you have ever flown in an airplane, you have probably seen that above the clouds, the haze, or the rain, the sky is always vast and clear, and looks utterly ordinary. In the same way, even when thoughts and emotions obscure it, the buddha nature is always vast and clear. It may look quite ordinary, and yet all its qualities — clarity, emptiness, and compassion — are contained within it.

Objectless calm-abiding meditation is the most basic method of resting the mind. You do not need to watch thoughts or emotions (I will explain that contemplative practice later), nor do you need to try to stop them. Simply rest in awareness with a child’s innocence, and watch the mind do its work, counting like a child: “Wow! Look at all the thoughts, sense perceptions, and emotions! They are coming and going within my awareness!”

In a sense, objectless calm-abiding meditation is a bit like gazing at the open sky rather than fixing your attention on the galaxies, celestial bodies, and planets moving through it. The coming and going of thoughts, emotions, and sense perceptions within awareness is like the movement of galaxies and stars through space. Just as we would not define space by the objects moving through it, so the thoughts and emotions and objects that awareness perceives cannot define or limit awareness itself. Awareness is simply “thusness,” and what objectless calm-abiding meditation means is resting in the thusness of awareness. Some people find this exercise very easy and others find it very difficult; this has to do with a person’s character, not with ability or skill.

This teaching is very simple. If you are doing formal meditation, it is best to use the seven-point posture of Vairocana as far as you are able. When you cannot use the seven-point posture — while driving or walking, for example — simply straighten your spine, relax your whole body, keep your balance, and let the mind relax into the sheer awareness of the present moment.

Inevitably, all kinds of thoughts, sense perceptions, and feelings will arise in our minds. This is bound to happen, because you have not yet learned to rest the mind. It is like going to the gym to lift weights: at first, after just a few pounds and a few repetitions, your muscles are tired. But if you keep practicing, gradually you will find that you can lift more weight and do more repetitions.

In the same way, learning to meditate is a gradual process. At first you may be able to settle for only a few seconds before all sorts of thoughts, emotions, and sense perceptions come surging in. The basic instruction is simply not to follow these thoughts and emotions, but to notice as they are whatever comes and goes within awareness. Whatever thoughts arise and fall in your mind, do not make too much of them and do not try to suppress them; just watch them come and go.

Once you start chasing after a thought, you can no longer recognize clearly what is happening in the present, and from there you begin to spin out all kinds of illusions, commentary, memories, and storylines that have nothing whatsoever to do with present reality. The more you let your mind wander after these thoughts, the further you drift from the openness and vastness of the present.

The purpose of calm-abiding meditation is to slowly and gradually break this habit and to keep present awareness, receiving all the possibilities of the present with an open heart. When you notice that you are chasing a thought, do not be hard on yourself or blame yourself. After all, you have already noticed that you are lingering in the past or thinking about the future, and that very noticing is enough to bring you back to the present and to strengthen your intention to meditate. In calm-abiding practice, your motivation to meditate is the crucial and decisive factor.

When you begin to meditate, take it slowly. My father used to tell all his new students, myself included, very carefully that the most effective way to begin is to rest the mind many times a day, but for short periods each time. Otherwise, he said, you may find meditation increasingly boring or become disappointed in your progress, and in the end simply give up. This approach of short periods and many repetitions is like the old saying: “Drop by drop, the jar is filled.”
So when you first begin to meditate, do not aim too high and insist on meditating for

minutes. Instead, set your goal at one minute, or even half a minute. Take the moments when you are willing or eager to pause in the midst of a busy life, and rather than letting yourself daydream, use those few seconds to observe your own mind. Practicing “little by little” in this way, you will find yourself gradually breaking free of the mental and emotional shackles that are the source of exhaustion, disappointment, anger, and despair. And then you will discover the infinite source of clarity, wisdom, diligence, tranquility, and compassion that was in your mind all along.
Focus single-pointedly on one particular object, and in this way rest the mind.
— The Ninth Gyalwang Karmapa, Mahāmudrā: Ocean of Definitive Meaning

When I first began formal meditation, I found that objectless meditation was difficult precisely because it was so simple. The nature of mind — awareness — is so close that it is very hard to recognize. From the moment we wake in the morning, wherever we go, whatever we eat, right up until we get ready for bed at night, awareness is always there. It is our innate cognizance, yet because it accompanies us every single moment, we fail to recognize how precious it is — to say nothing of how easily we fall prey to thoughts, feelings, and sense perceptions, the by-products that the mind naturally produces.
If you find yourself facing this problem, you are not alone.

Fortunately, my father and my other teachers were thoroughly familiar with the difficulties that arise in resting the mind directly, and they were able to teach others more gradual techniques. The simplest of these is to use our senses directly to settle and relax the mind.
The whole world is the world of mind, the masterpiece of mind.
— Chögyam Trungpa Rinpoche, The Heart of the Buddha

Like scientists, Buddhists have some understanding of the five sense perceptions: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. In Buddhist terminology they are called “the doors of perception,” rather like the doors and windows of a house. Most of our feelings and perceived objects come about through the functioning of one or more of the senses, and in this way they shape our experience. However, since these five sense perceptions, or what Buddhist texts call the “five sense consciousnesses,” can enter only the objects that the senses perceive, Buddhist science goes on to speak of a sixth consciousness, the “mental consciousness.” (In ordinary usage, “consciousness” refers to the mental capacity that can recognize and think. For example, we say that a person in a coma has lost “consciousness.” But in Buddhist terminology, “mental consciousness” has a specific meaning: it refers to one of the six capacities of mind for cognizing objects. These six capacities of mind are called the “six consciousnesses”: eye consciousness, ear consciousness, nose consciousness, tongue consciousness, body consciousness, and mental consciousness. The objects that the six can respectively discern are: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile sensations, and thoughts. Generally speaking, each consciousness can discern only its own object; the mental consciousness relies on the objects of the other five and can discern only thoughts and ideas, not directly discern forms, sounds, or smells. Take the process of the eye seeing a bottle: first eye consciousness, through the eye, discerns the shape and color of some object, and only then, through the mental consciousness, does one discern the thought “this is a bottle.”) The sixth consciousness is nothing mysterious, and has nothing to do with superpowers or clairvoyance. “Mental consciousness” is simply one capacity of mind, one that allows us to recognize and distinguish what we see, smell, hear, taste, or touch.

Buddhist tradition compares these six consciousnesses to a house with five doors, one on each of four sides and one in the roof. These five doors represent the five sense consciousnesses. Now suppose someone puts a monkey into this house; the monkey here stands for the mental consciousness. Suddenly placed in a big house, the monkey naturally goes wild with excitement, dashing and leaping all over the place and running to every doorway to see whether there is anything new, special, or interesting. Whatever this crazy monkey finds, it immediately judges by its own experience to be pleasant or painful, good or bad, or merely boring. People passing by the house see a monkey at every door and assume there are five monkeys inside, but in fact there is only one — that restless, untrained “mental consciousness.” Yet, like every other sentient being, this crazy monkey really only wants to be happy and to be free from suffering. So we can teach the crazy monkey in our own mind to calm down by deliberately focusing on different senses.
To pacify our ceaseless habit of fabrication, the Buddhas teach us to rely on an object of focus.
Once we grow accustomed to this object, our attention becomes stable.
— Tulku Urgyen Rinpoche, As It Is

In everyday experience, almost all the information we receive through our senses becomes a source of distraction, because our minds are in the habit of fixating on the information of sense perception. At the same time, because we are embodied beings, if we try to free ourselves entirely from the senses or to block the information they receive, we are bound to experience a sense of powerlessness.

A more practical approach is to make friends with our senses and to use the information they receive as a way of resting the mind. Buddhist scriptures call this process “applying the antidote to itself,” that is, using the very source of distraction as the antidote to distraction. This analogy comes from an ancient and common practice: using a material of the same kind to work that material. If you want to cut glass, for instance, you use a tool made of glass; if you want to cut iron, you must use an iron tool. By the same logic, you can use your own senses as the antidote to sensory distraction.

In “meditation with an object,” we use our senses as the means of resting the mind. We can use the eye faculty to meditate on shapes and colors, the ear faculty to meditate on sounds, the nose faculty to meditate on smells, the tongue faculty to meditate on tastes, and the body faculty to meditate on bodily sensations. In this way, the various kinds of information received through the senses become precious resources for our practice.

After I learned to observe what I perceived in a calm and contemplative way, practice became much easier. I found that I grew less and less emotional about everything I perceived. In place of the earlier thought, “Hey, that guy is yelling at me!” I could think, “Well, this person’s voice is rather loud and his tone is a bit sharp; the sound he is making is probably meant to insult or hurt someone.”

In other words, simply by learning to rest my attention lightly on the information received by my senses, free of the emotional and semantic charge that came with the other person’s voice, he could no longer harm me. And because I could listen to him without any defensiveness, I found I could respond with a more open heart, which dissolved his anger while costing me nothing of my dignity.

When you begin “calm-abiding meditation with an object,” one of the easiest approaches is to rest your attention gently on simple bodily sensations. Simply focus your attention on a particular area, the forehead, for example.

To begin, straighten your spine and relax your body. For formal meditation you may use the seven-point posture described earlier. If the place you are in is not suited to the seven-point posture, then simply straighten your spine and let your whole body relax comfortably. During meditation it does not matter whether your eyes are open or closed, though some people find that closing their eyes is more helpful. (Of course, if you are driving or walking down the street, I strongly suggest you keep your eyes open!)
Let your mind rest as it is for a few seconds
Now slowly move your awareness to your forehead
You may feel some tingling or warmth, perhaps even a slight itch or a sense of pressure. Whatever you feel, simply become aware of it for a minute or two
Simply notice it
Just gently rest your attention on the sensation
Then let go of your attention and let your mind rest as it is. If your eyes are closed, you can open them now.
How did that feel?

After you have spent a little time resting your awareness on one part of the body, you can extend the technique by slowly shifting and bringing your attention to the whole body. Sometimes I call this practice of whole-body sensation the “scanning practice,” because it reminds me of lying inside a machine for a full-body scan. Again, for formal meditation use the seven-point posture described earlier; for informal practice in daily life, simply straighten your spine and let your whole body relax naturally and comfortably. Either way, you may close your eyes or keep them open, whichever feels comfortable to you.

To begin, first rest for a while in objectless calm-abiding meditation, then slowly move your awareness to whatever sensation is present at your forehead. Let your mind simply observe these sensations, just simply aware, nothing more. Then gradually move your focus downward and go on observing the various sensations of your face, neck, shoulders, and arms

and the sensations there; simply observe them, without needing to stop any state that arises in the mind or to change the object you are observing. Just keep body and mind relaxed and calm, and when sensations arise, simply recognize them. After observing in this way for a few minutes, let your mind simply rest, then return to observing your sensations. Keep alternating in this way between the practice of “observing” (with an object) and “resting the mind” (without an object).

Most of our sensations are related in some way to the body. In daily life our body is always in contact with the outside world — the chair we sit on, the floor, a pen, our clothes, an animal, or another person — and different contacts produce different bodily sensations. In Buddhist terminology, the sensations that come from direct bodily contact are called “coarse sensations” (rough bodily sensations). But the more deeply you attend to what you are feeling, the more you begin to recognize feelings that are not necessarily related to touch; these are called “subtle sensations” (subtle bodily sensations).

When I first practiced this calm-abiding technique, I found that whenever I tried to avoid a sensation, it grew stronger. But if I simply looked at it, then no matter how uncomfortable it was, it became easier to bear.

As a curious child, I naturally had to know why this transformation happened. Just watching the process for a while, I understood: when I let myself simply observe a sensation, I was wholeheartedly engaged in whatever situation was unfolding in the present, and this showed me that one part of my mind was resisting the painful feeling while another part was urging me to look at it objectively. Watching these two contradictory impulses arise at the same time, I could see my mind working through the middle ground between “avoidance” and “acceptance.” As it turned out, being aware of the mind’s activity became far more interesting than either “avoiding” or “accepting.” Watching my own mind in action was absolutely fascinating! I think this is the most practical definition I can give of “clarity”: clarity is the ability to observe the mind operating on several levels at once.

blocks.text: Meditation Using Pain as a Support

inline.s: The sensations of cold, heat, hunger, fullness, heaviness, dizziness, headache, toothache, a blocked nose, a sore throat, aching knees, or a pain in the lower back are not always pleasant, but our awareness takes them in just this directly. Because painful and uncomfortable sensations are so immediate, they are in fact very effective objects for meditation.

Most people regard pain as a great threat to the comfort of the body. On the one hand, when we feel anxious about or troubled by this threat, the pain almost always grows stronger; on the other hand, if we treat the pain or the discomfort as an object of meditation and simply watch how the mind handles all manner of problems, then we can use these sensations to enhance the clarity of the mind.

For example, when I am in formal meditation, or simply sitting in a car or an airplane, and I feel a little pain in my leg or my back, I directly watch the mind's experience of the pain, instead of stretching, standing up, or fidgeting; after all, this is merely consciousness recognizing and distinguishing a sensation.

When I turn my attention to the mind that experiences the pain, rather than concentrating on some point of ache, the pain may not necessarily disappear, but it allows me to participate actively in the experience that is happening right now, instead of trying to escape it. The same principle holds for pleasant sensations. I do not attempt to prolong these sensations, but simply observe the manifesting of these joyful experiences. In fact, the training of my early years taught me how to use sensory perception as a tool for examining and grasping the boundless potential of my own mind, rather than being used in turn by sensory perception, which would strengthen a confining sense of being bound by the body.

Of course, if you suffer from chronic or severe pain, you should go to a doctor, because these symptoms may be the sign of a serious illness. But I have heard that when the doctor has ruled out the possibility of a major illness, the pain they had been feeling has actually lessened. It seems that the fear of pain appears to intensify the pain and deepen its sense of reality, and this may be a self-reinforcing red alert transmitted from the thalamus to the amygdala and other parts of the brain. However, if the doctor truly diagnoses a serious illness, then you must absolutely follow the doctor's instructions for treatment. Although meditation can help you face the pain and discomfort that a serious illness brings, it cannot replace medical treatment.

After taking the doctor's prescription or an over-the-counter medicine from the pharmacy, you may still feel some pain; at such a time you can try to use these physical pains as a support for meditation. If your pain comes from a serious illness, then when using pain as a support for meditation, be careful not to have expectations about the outcome of the practice. If your hidden motive is to get rid of the pain, then you are in fact reinforcing the neural pattern that fears the pain. The best way to weaken this neural pattern is to make an effort to observe the pain objectively, while letting go of the result.

The incident that truly impressed me with this teaching was a small operation my father underwent in Germany. Before the operation, the anesthesiologist should first have injected anesthetic into the affected area, but because the anesthesiologist was busy with affairs, he completely forgot about my father. Therefore, when the doctor made the first incision, he noticed that the muscle of the affected area began to convulse; if the area had already been anesthetized, this would certainly not have happened. The doctor flew into a rage at the anesthesiologist's dereliction, but my father asked him to let the matter rest, because my father had felt no pain at all. My father explained to the doctor that the sensation of this extremely sensitive area being cut open instead offered an opportunity to raise his awareness to a state of great clarity and peace.

In short, through practice my father had developed a network of neural connections that naturally converted the experience of pain into “an objective observation by the mind of the sensation of pain.” Although the doctor insisted on applying anesthetic to the affected area before continuing the operation, because of my father's insistence the doctor did not press charges against the woman in charge of the anesthesia. The next day, the anesthesiologist came to my father's bedside, smiled, and thanked my father for having gotten him out of trouble, and then produced from behind his back a large bag of snacks; my father found them quite tasty.

This exercise of observing the sensations of the body, whether “coarse sensations” or “subtle sensations,” is quite simple. You can practice it during formal meditation, or at any time during the day, whether during a meeting, a gathering, or in the intervals of other necessary activities, in the few seconds you can seize. In fact, I personally find this practice especially useful in daily life, because it produces a sense of immediate ease and openness. Some people have told me that they find this practice very helpful at work, especially when they have to sit for a long time listening to lengthy reports.

blocks.text: Meditation Using Form as a Support

inline.s: The method of meditation in which one calms the mind using visual faculty as a support is called “form meditation.” But do not be put off by this technical term; form meditation is actually very simple. In fact, we do this practice unconsciously every day, for example, when we stare at a computer screen or a traffic sign. If we turn this unconscious process into active awareness and deliberately place our attention on a particular object, then our mind becomes very peaceful, very broad, and relaxed.

I began by learning with small objects that I could see effortlessly, whether a patch of color on the floor, a candle flame, a photograph, or even the back of the head of the person sitting in front of me in class. You can also use objects of spiritual significance, which are usually called “pure images.” If you are a Buddhist, you can use an image of the Buddha or a Dharma photograph; if you are a Christian, you can concentrate on a cross or the portrait of a saint; if you follow another religion, then you may choose an object with special significance for yourself to practice with. When you become more adept at this practice, you can even concentrate on a form in the mind, that is, an object recalled to mind.

Whatever object you choose, you may notice that it has two characteristics: shape and color. You can choose either one and decide which to concentrate on; whether it is white, black, or pink, or a round, square, or many-angled object, anything will do. The point is to place your attention on the color or shape, to throw your consciousness onto it just enough to detect the object, and that is all; it is that simple. When you place your attention on this object, you are aware.

You do not need to see every detail of this object clearly and distinctly; to do so would only make you tense, whereas the point of this practice is to abide easily. Make the focus of your attention a little loose, just enough to maintain the bare awareness of the object seen. Do not try to produce any result, and do not force your mind to relax; just think simply: “All right! Whatever is to happen, let it happen! This is meditation, and this is what I am doing.” Do not think of anything else.

Of course, there is also the possibility that you stare wide-eyed at the object and yet see nothing at all. Your mind may be entirely drawn away by a distant sound, so for a few seconds, or even a few minutes, you have not seen the object at all. I really dislike how my mind drifts like this! But my father also said that the state of the mind drifting is perfectly natural. When you notice that your mind has moved away from the object of focus, just bring your attention back to the object. And so, I encourage you to try practicing right now.

Choose a posture in which you feel most comfortable, and let your mind abide in a state of ease and comfort for a while. Then choose some object that you see, and rest your gaze on this object, noting its shape or color. You do not need to stare fixedly at it; blink whenever you need to. In fact, if you do not blink at all, your eyes may become dry and irritated. After gazing at this object for a while, let your mind simply relax again, then place your attention back on the object for a few minutes, then let the mind relax once more.
Whenever I use a visible object as a support for meditation, I recall the words of the great fourteenth
-century

Buddhist scholar and meditation master Longchenpa. In one of his works he pointed out that it is extremely beneficial to alternate between meditation with an object and meditation without an object. He explained that when you rest your mind on some object, you regard it as something different from or distinct from yourself. But when you let go of the object and simply rest your mind in the bare awareness, this distinction dissolves.

By alternating in this way between “concentrating on an object” and “let the mind rest in bare awareness,” you will begin to experience the fundamental truth of which neuroscientists speak: everything we perceive is in fact only a reconstruction produced in the mind. In other words, the object seen and the mind that sees are not distinct from each other.

Of course, such realization does not come at once; one must spend some effort to practice it. In fact, as we shall understand a little later, the Buddha taught certain special methods to dissolve the distinction between the mind and the object received by the mind. But I have gotten ahead of myself here; this is what happens every time I get excited. Now, let us return to the basic method of converting sensory information into the calming of the mind.

blocks.text: Meditation Using Sound as a Support

inline.s: Meditation using sound as a support” is very similar to “meditation using form as a support,” except that now you use the ear faculty.

First, let your mind abide in a relaxed state for a while, then gradually become aware of the sounds heard by the ears, such as the sound of your own heartbeat or breathing, or all the sounds that arise naturally around you. Some people find that playing natural music or light music is also very helpful. You do not need to identify these sounds, nor do you need to concentrate on any particular one. In fact, it is easier to simply be aware of all the sounds you hear; the point is to cultivate a simple, bare awareness of sound when sound touches the ear.

Just as in meditating on form, you may find that you can only concentrate on sound for a few seconds before the mind wanders about. That is fine; when you notice that your mind has scattered, return to a relaxed state, and then move your awareness back to the sound. In this way alternate between concentrating on the sound and letting the mind rest in an open, relaxed state.

One of the great benefits of meditation using sound as a support is that it will slowly teach you to listen to all kinds of sounds with detachment, without defining these sounds; thus you begin to learn to hear sounds without reacting emotionally to their content. As you gradually grow accustomed to being aware that “sound is merely sound,” you will find that you can listen to criticism without anger or defensiveness, and hear praise without excessive pride or excitement. In this way, you can listen to others in a more relaxed and neutral attitude, without being led about by emotional reactions.

I once heard a wonderful story about how a famous Indian sitar master learned to use the sound of the instrument as a support for meditation. If you are not familiar with Indian instruments, let me explain first. The sitar is an instrument with a long neck, and it usually has seventeen

strings, and like a guitar it produces all manner of beautiful sounds. This sitar master was extremely skilled, and people all over India would invite him to play, so like many modern rock bands he was always on tour and almost never had time to stay at home.

After an especially long tour, he returned to his homeland and discovered that his wife was having an affair. Even so, the sitar master remained very calm; perhaps it was the concentration gained from years of practicing and performing, or the sound of this moving instrument, that kept his mind both settled and focused. In any case, he did not quarrel with his wife, nor did he fly into a rage; instead he sat down with his wife and talked for a long time. In the course of the conversation he realized that his wife's affair and his own pride arising from being invited all over the country on tour were both expressions of attachment, one of the three poisons that make us mired in the wheel of samsara; his attachment to fame and his wife's attachment to her lover were no different from each other.

This realization struck him like a thunderbolt, and he understood that if he wished to free himself from this clinging, he would have to let go of his attachment to fame; and the only way was to find a meditation master and learn how to recognize that attachment is merely one manifestation of a habit of the mind.

After the two had finished talking, he gave all his possessions to his wife, keeping only the sitar at his side, because he still had a strong attachment to it, and no amount of rational analysis could remove such attachment; then he set out to seek a teacher.

Finally he came to a charnel ground, an ancient cemetery. In the charnel ground, the corpses were mostly discarded on the ground at random, neither cremated nor buried. This was a ghastly place, strewn with human bones, broken skeletons, and half-rotted corpses. But here it was most possible to find a meditation master who had overcome the fears of death and impermanence. If one could not overcome these two fearful states, one would continually cling to whatever lay before one and resist the unknown future, and thus be unable to free oneself from samsara.

In this charnel ground the sitar player finally found a mahasiddha, a great adept, whose Sanskrit meaning is “one who has gone through all manner of extraordinary trials and attained profound realization.” This great adept lived in a run-down hut that barely sheltered him from wind and rain. Just as when we meet certain people in daily life and immediately feel a deep connection with them, such was the impression the sitar player had of this great adept; he asked the master whether he would accept him as a disciple, and the master consented. The sitar player then built his own hut near the master's dwelling with branches and mud, and began to practice the basic teachings of calm-abiding meditation the master had taught him.

Like many beginning meditation students, the sitar player found it very difficult to follow the teacher's instructions; even when he obediently did as the teacher told him, after sitting only a few minutes it felt as if he had sat for a lifetime. Every time he sat down to meditate, he found himself led about by the old habit of playing the instrument, and then he would set his meditation aside and begin to play. This made him feel extremely guilty, because he was neglecting his meditation and preferring just to play his sitar. Finally he went to the master's hut to confess, saying that he simply could not calm himself to meditate.
What is the problem?” the great adept asked him.
The sitar player replied: “I am too attached to my sitar; I would rather play than meditate.”
The great adept then told him: “This is not a big problem. I can teach you how to meditate with the sitar.”
The sitar player had expected a scolding from the teacher — as most of us do when facing a teacher — but the teacher's words surprised him greatly.
The great adept went on: “Go back to your hut and play your sitar; whether you play well or not does not matter, just listen to the sound of the instrument with your bare awareness.”

The sitar player, greatly relieved, returned to his hut and began to play. He listened to the sound of the instrument, without seeking whether his playing was perfect, and without expecting any result from the playing or the practice. Because he had learned to practice simply, without expecting results, a few years later he too became a great adept.

Not many of my students are sitar players, so the moral of this story is in fact to teach us how to make good use of our own experiences as a support for practice, without expecting any result from the practice. Especially the sounds, sights, and smells of the Western rush hour can all become a rich support for meditation. Do not simply make up your mind to cross the teeming street; observe well the various sensations of the traffic jam; such practice is a great opportunity for meditation. If you can shift your attention from hurrying to get somewhere to resting in the sensations around you, then you may well become a “maestro of the traffic jam.”

blocks.text: Meditation Using Smell as a Support

inline.s: In fact, at any time one can use whatever sensation most attracts us at the moment as an object of meditation. For instance, using smell as an object of meditation; this object is very useful whether in formal meditation or in daily activities. In formal meditation, you can concentrate your attention on the smells around you, perhaps the scent of incense (if you like it), or the scents that arise naturally near the place of practice.

In everyday life, smell is especially practical as a support for meditation when cooking or eating. With just a little effort, learning to concentrate your attention on the smell of food, you can in fact transform such dull routines as cooking, eating, or even walking back and forth in an office building into a practice that calms the mind and strengthens mental power.
Meditation Using Taste as a Support

It took me a long time to discover that when I was eating or drinking, I rarely noticed what I was doing; I was usually busy talking with others, or distracted by my own problems, conflicts, or daydreams. As a result, I was not at all engaged in what I was doing at the moment, and completely missed the experience of the present feeling.
Concentrating on taste is a very practical meditation technique; we can take the several opportunities of breakfast, lunch, and dinner each day to meditate.

When learning to use taste as the object of focus, first, likewise let the mind rest naturally for a while, then gently focus your attention on the taste you are experiencing, without needing to analyze whether it is bitter, sweet, or sour. Just gently rest your attention on all the tastes you experience, and then let the mind rest naturally; that is, alternate between the two steps of placing attention on the awareness of taste and letting the mind rest naturally.
In order to guide my disciples well, I have taught many different Dharma-gates.
— The Lankavatara Sutra

In addition to meditation using the sense faculties as objects, the Buddha also taught other meditation techniques that can be easily taken up anywhere at any time; one of these is using the breath as an object of meditation.

As long as you are alive, you must breathe, so meditation that directs attention to the breath is always useful. Another auxiliary method is an old friend of mine, and one I am especially grateful for, for if not for it I might have gone mad as a child. This support is a fine method I discovered by chance while sitting in a cave, and that is the recitation of mantra.

I have learned many methods of using the (in-and-out) breath as an object of meditation, but I will not enumerate them all here; I will only speak of the two simplest. These two methods are not only the easiest to practice, but in public they will not cause people to give you the “stare.” You need only gently place your attention on the simple act of inhaling and exhaling; you can concentrate on the air entering your body through the nostrils, or focus your attention on the sensation of air entering and leaving the lungs. This method of meditation using the breath is very similar to the meditation on bodily sensations mentioned earlier. The difference is that here we narrow the scope of awareness, focusing only on the experience of inhaling and exhaling. Since there is a naturally brief interval between exhaling and inhaling, you can also concentrate on the three parts: inhaling, exhaling, and the interval.

This method of concentrating on the breath is especially useful when we are tense or scattered. Observing the simple act of the breath can create in the mind a state of stability and awareness, allowing you to step back and see clearly the difficulty before you at the moment, and to respond more calmly and objectively. When you are overwhelmed by stress, just place your attention on the breath; no one will notice that you are meditating, and perhaps not even notice whether you are still breathing.

Formal meditation using the breath as a support is somewhat different. One of the methods I learned is to make the attention even more completely concentrated by counting the breath (counting the number of breaths). That is, count the first inhale and exhale as “one,” the next inhale and exhale as “two,” and so on, until you count to “seven,” then begin again from “one.” Afterwards you can increase the count, but as we mentioned earlier, it is best at the outset to set the practice time to something short, so that you can repeat the practice many times.

Meditating with mantra is an extremely powerful technique; not only can it cultivate clear awareness, but through the power of these mantras which the realized masters have recited for thousands of years, it can also help us purify the layers of mental obscurations and increase our capacity to benefit both self and others. Such a connection may at first be hard to accept, because it is too much like magic. But we can think of a mantra as sound waves that have been reverberating in space for thousands, or even millions, of years; then it is much easier to accept.

When meditating with mantra, your attention is concentrated on a set of recitations that seem to have a direct effect of calming and purifying the mind. The practice we are going to do now uses a simple mantra composed of three syllables, the basis of all mantras: Om (
OM
), Ah (
AH)
), and Hum (
HUNG

). “Om” represents the clear, distinct, and aware dimension of experience; “Ah” represents emptiness, or the innate vast openness; and “Hum” represents the indivisible union of the various appearances and their empty nature.

At the beginning, you can recite aloud, then gradually turn into inner silent recitation; the point is to keep silently reciting the mantra for about three minutes, then let the mind rest. In this way alternate between reciting and resting, for as long as you can. Whether or not you immediately feel the effect, the seed of freeing your own mind has already sprouted at this moment.

But liberation rarely arrives in the form we think; in fact, for most people, liberation is not only unfamiliar but evidently an unpleasant notion. This is because we are so used to our chains; these chains may chafe our skin, may make us bleed, but at least they are what we are familiar with.

However, familiarity is only a thought, and sometimes only a feeling. To help us pass through the difficult transformation from familiarity to liberation, the Buddha gave various teachings that directly use thoughts and feelings.

blocks.text: Four: Making Good Use of Thoughts and Emotions

inline.s: Cast longing behind you, cut off attachment from its root!
— Jamgon Kongtrul Lodro Taye, The Torch of Definitive Meaning
Long, long ago, in India there was a cowherd who spent most of his life tending cattle for his master. At about sixty

years of age, he finally woke up: “This is really a boring job, every single day the same routine of leading the cattle to the pasture, watching them graze, and taking them home. What can I learn from this?” After thinking for a while, he decided to give up his work and go learn how to meditate, so that at least he might free himself from the wheel of samsara.

After giving up his work, he wandered about. One day he saw a great adept sitting in a cave. The moment he saw this great adept, the cowherd felt boundless joy in his heart, so he went up and asked the master how he should meditate. The master taught him the basic meditation instruction using thoughts as a support. After receiving the teaching, the cowherd found a cave nearby, settled himself, and began to practice.

Like most of us, the cowherd immediately encountered a problem. Having herded cattle for decades, he had developed feelings for the animals, and every time he tried to practice what the great adept had taught him, he would keep thinking of the cattle he had cared for. Although he struggled hard to block these thoughts, the images of the cattle kept appearing in his mind; the more he tried to remove these thoughts, the clearer the images of the cattle became.

After exhausting himself, he finally went to report to the master that these teachings were truly too difficult for him. The great adept asked him where the problem lay, and he explained his difficulty in full detail.
This is not a big problem,” the master told him, “I can teach you another method; it is called ‘cow meditation.’”
What?” the cowherd said, astonished.

I mean it,” the great adept replied, “you only need to watch the images of the herd that appear in your mind. Watch yourself, as before, leading them to the pasture, watching them graze, and then bringing them back to the farm. Whatever thoughts about cattle arise, just watch these thoughts.”

So the cowherd returned to his cave and sat down to practice the new instruction. Since he no longer tried to block his thoughts, this time his meditation went very smoothly. He began to feel an extraordinary peace and joy, no longer longing for his cattle, and his mind became more and more settled, calm, and gentle.
After a while, he went back to the great adept and asked: “Now that I have completed the cow meditation, what should I do next?”
The master replied: “Very good, you have learned how to calm your mind. Now I will teach you the second stage of the cow meditation. The teaching is this: visualize your own body as a cow.”
So the cowherd returned to his cave and began to practice this teaching, thinking: “All right, now I am a cow; I have a pair of horns and four hooves, I moo, I eat grass

” The more he practiced this, the more he found his mind becoming more peaceful and joyful than ever. Believing he had mastered this practice, the cowherd went back to the master and asked whether there was a third stage of instruction.
Yes,” the great master replied slowly, “for the third-stage ox-meditation you must focus intently on the thought that you have a pair of horns.”

The cowherd returned to his cave and, following his teacher’s instructions, meditated on nothing but the thought that he had a pair of horns. He concentrated single-mindedly on the size, the position, and the color of the horns, and on the feeling of the two horns’ weight pressing against the sides of his head. He practiced like this for several months. Then one morning, waking, he decided to go out of the cave to relieve himself; but as he stepped out he felt something on his head catching against the rock on both sides of the cave mouth, so that he could not get through. He touched his head to see what was caught, and to his astonishment discovered that two long horns had actually grown out of it.
Turning sideways, he managed with great difficulty to squeeze himself out of the cave, and then, frightened and amazed, ran off to find his teacher.
Look what has happened!” he shouted. “You told me to practice the ox-meditation, and now I have truly grown horns! How terrifying—this is just like a nightmare!”

The great master laughed with delight. “Not terrifying at all—this is wonderful!” he said loudly. “You have mastered the third stage of the ox-meditation. Now you must do the fourth stage. You must think: ‘Now I am not an ox, and I have no horns on my head.’”
Obediently the cowherd returned to his cave and practiced the fourth stage of the ox-meditation, thinking “now I have no horns, now I have no horns, now I have no horns
After a few days of practice, one morning when he got up he found he could walk easily out of the cave; the horns on his head had disappeared.

Surprised, he ran to the master and reported, “Look, I no longer have horns on my head! What is going on? When I thought there were horns on my head, horns grew; when I thought there were no horns, they disappeared. Whatever can be the reason?”

The great master answered, “The appearance and disappearance of the horns are both due to the difference in what your own mind focuses upon. The power of the mind is immeasurably strong: it can make experience appear very real, and it can equally make it appear very unreal.”
So it is!” said the cowherd.

The master went on to explain: “Horns are not the only thing that appears or disappears by the focus of one’s own mind. In truth, everything is like this—your body, other people, even this whole world. The nature of all things is emptiness; none really exists. Everything is merely an object taken by your own mind, and to recognize this is to truly ‘see.’ First you must quiet your own mind, and then learn to see things as they really are. Next comes the fifth stage of the ox-meditation, learning to balance both stillness and right view.”

The cowherd again returned to his cave and meditated with stillness and right view. A few years later he himself became a great master: his mind had grown settled, and he was freed from the painful round of samsara.

There are hardly any cowherds nowadays, otherwise the world might be a somewhat calmer place. But if you are bold enough, you might try the cowherd’s meditation method, only using a different object of focus—say, a car. After practicing the car-meditation for a few years, you too might become a great master like the old cowherd. Of course, you must be willing to spend some years growing headlights, doors, and seat belts, perhaps even a trunk, and then learn to make these things disappear. While doing such practice, you may find it hard to get in and out of the office elevator. And if, when a colleague asks you a question, you answer with a honk of the horn instead of human speech, they may find that a little odd.
Of course, this is only a joke! There are, in fact, other and simpler ways of working with thoughts that do not require actually learning to grow horns or rear lights.
When a thought arises, do not treat it as a deficiency,
but recognize it as empty, and let it present itself as it is.
Guru Gampopa, The Supreme Continuum

Even after you have become good friends with your five senses and have learned to use the information they receive as a support for meditation, you may still find that “excited, crazy monkey” rather hard to handle. This monkey stands for our consciousness, which is always leaping about, randomly manufacturing confusion, doubt, and uncertainty. Even when you have learned to rest in simple sensory awareness, the crazy monkey-mind keeps finding new ways to create disorder—say, by offering all manner of disturbing interpretations, doing its best to interrupt the stability, clarity, and openness you have attained. It is a bit like having a pillow fight in your head, or snatching food from an altar.

The crazy monkey may be hard to deal with, but its mischief is not a “bad” thing; it is only a deeply entrenched neural pattern trying to grab the limelight. This crazy monkey was originally a neural response that humans developed to face survival threats. So when you meet the crazy monkey, rather than getting angry with it, it is better to make good use of its presence. Why not feel gratitude toward its workings, thanking it for letting us survive?

However, after you have learned to work with your senses, you must begin to deal with this crazy monkey. The trick is to use the thoughts and emotions that the crazy monkey produces as a support for settling your own mind. Once you can work seamlessly with these thoughts and emotions, you will begin to discover that you can be entirely freed from the age-old survival-response patterns. And this whole process begins with questioning whether every thought and every feeling you have is a fact or a habit.

The first lessons we learn in life are usually the most important: for example, “look both ways before crossing the street,” “don’t take candy from strangers,” “don’t play with matches.” Children hear these reminders, meant for their own good, over and over from their parents. Yet however important these warnings may be, they always seem to go in one ear and out the other. Human nature is like this: we love to take risks—that is how we learn life’s lessons—but some lessons can cost a life, and others can cause lifelong wounds. So even as adults, we must again and again review the lessons we learned in childhood and pass them on to the next generation; meaningful lessons are worth repeating.

So please forgive this repetition of what I learned in my own early formal training—that thinking is a natural activity of the mind, that meditation is not a matter of suppressing your thoughts but a process of resting the mind in its natural state, and of accepting thoughts, emotions, and sensory perceptions with complete openness as they manifest, naturally aware of them. The mind is like a river; precisely because it is like a river, trying to stop the flow of water is pointless. You might as well try to stop your heartbeat, or keep your lungs from breathing—would that help?

But this does not mean you must become a slave to the mind. When you do not understand the nature and origin of your thoughts, these thoughts use you. When the Buddha recognized the nature of his own mind, he reversed this process. He showed us how to make good use of our thoughts rather than be used by them.

When I began my father’s formal training, I was very nervous. I was sure he must have seen how restless my mind was, how many crazy thoughts were flowing through it every second. With faculties so poor, he was certain to send me away. In one sense I guessed right: he did indeed see how wild my mind was. But that my faculties were too poor to learn meditation—there I guessed wrong.

My father told me and the other students that it did not matter how many thoughts passed through the mind during meditation. If a hundred thoughts passed through your mind in a minute’s interval, then you had a hundred supports for meditation. “How fortunate you are!” he once said. “If the crazy monkey in your head is leaping about all over the place, that is wonderful—just watch it make its mischief. Every leap, every thought, every disturbance, just like a sense object, is a support for meditation. When you find yourself struggling against many disturbances, you can in fact make use of each disturbance as the object of meditation; then these disturbances are no longer disturbances but supports for your meditation.”

But he also warned us that when thoughts arise, we should not try to grasp every one of them. Whatever thoughts pass through the mind, just watch them come and go—lightly, without clinging—just as before, when we practiced resting our attention gently on a sight, a sound, or a smell.

Watching thoughts is a little like catching a bus. You arrive at the stop just as the bus is pulling away, so you have to wait for the next one. Likewise, between one thought and the next there is usually a gap, perhaps shorter than an instant but a gap nonetheless. This gap is the experience of the completely open natural mind; then another thought jumps out, and when it disappears there is another gap, and then another thought comes and goes, followed by another gap.

The process of watching thoughts keeps cycling thus: after a thought comes a gap, immediately after the gap comes a thought, and then another gap. If you can keep practicing without pause, then gradually these gaps grow longer and longer, and your experience of resting in your own mind as it is becomes ever more direct. The mind thus has two basic states—one with thoughts and one without—and both are equally supports for meditation.

When you first practice, attention to thoughts always drifts. That is all right; when you notice that your mind has wandered, just let yourself be aware that your mind is wandering. If you can let your awareness gently seep into these thoughts, even daydreaming can become a support for meditation.
When you suddenly think, “Wow! I should be watching my thoughts, I should be focusing on a form, I should be listening to a sound

at that point simply draw the attention back to the object you should be focused on. The immediate experiences of these “Wow!” moments hold a great secret, for they are in fact fleeting experiences of your own nature.

If you could grasp every “Wow!” moment, that would be wonderful, but it is impossible. If you try to do so, they harden into concepts, and the immediate experience of “Wow!” becomes a concept about the immediate experience of “Wow!” The good news, however, is that the more you practice, the more likely you are to experience more “Wow!” moments. Gradually these immediate experiences of “Wow!” accumulate, until one day they become the mind’s natural state—a state freed from neural habits; and this natural state of mind lets you look at any thought, any feeling, and any situation with a wholly free openness.
Wow” is a wonderful thing.

Let us now practice the “Wow!” and place attention on “thoughts” as a support for meditation. As with the other exercises, first let the mind rest for a while in objectless awareness. This is very important; then begin to watch your thoughts. Do not try to practice too long—just let yourself watch your thoughts for a few minutes.
First, rest your mind for one minute
Then let your mind become aware of its own thoughts, perhaps for two minutes
Then rest your mind again for one minute

When you have finished, ask yourself what the experience was like. Were there many “Wow!” moments? Could you see your thoughts clearly? Or were they all dim and vague? Or, each time you tried to look at them, did they vanish like thin smoke blown by the wind?

When I teach this practice publicly, I always ask the audience about their experience, and the answers are as varied as can be. Some say that when they try to watch their thoughts, the thoughts themselves become a bit elusive—either vanishing at once or growing unclear. Others say their thoughts become very solid and distinct, appearing in the mind as words and sentences, and they can watch the thoughts come and go without clinging much or being much disturbed.

Now I am going to tell you a great secret, which is that there is really no secret at all! The two extremes people describe—thoughts vanishing or becoming clearer—and everything in between, are all experiences of meditation. If you are very afraid of your thoughts, then you are letting your thoughts control you, because they are to you so solid and real, as if truly real. The more you fear these thoughts, the more powerful they become. But when you begin to be aware of these thoughts, the power you yourself have given them gradually weakens, and then one of two things happens.

Sometimes, when you observe your thoughts closely, you begin to notice that they appear and vanish very quickly, with a small gap left between one thought and the next. At first the gap between thoughts may not be very long, but with continued practice these gaps grow longer and longer, and your mind is increasingly able to rest, still and open, in objectless meditation.

At other times, this simple practice of watching thoughts becomes a little like watching television or a film. There may be many storylines happening on the screen continuously, but you are not actually on the screen, are you? Between you and the images you are watching there is a small space; and when you practice watching your thoughts, you in fact also experience a certain small gap between yourself and your thoughts.

This gap is not something you make; it has always been there, and you are only letting yourself notice it. Because you become increasingly aware of this gap, you begin to be able to enjoy the process of watching thoughts. Even if some thoughts are truly frightening, you are neither swallowed nor controlled by them.

Thus, let the thoughts unfold in their own way, like an adult watching children play in the sand, or playing at war with toy soldiers, or at other games. The children throw themselves into their games with great energy, but the adult only watches their solemn, earnest doings and smiles fondly and gently.

Whatever experience arises is fine, and in practice the experiences will certainly change. Sometimes you watch your thoughts closely and carefully, seeing them come and go and perceiving the gaps between them; sometimes you just watch from a little distance. Meditation is actually far easier than people imagine. Whatever you are experiencing, so long as you can be aware of everything that is happening, that is meditation!

The only thing that moves you from the meditative state to another is when you try to control or change the present experience. However, if you can be aware that you are trying to control the present experience, that too is meditation.

Of course, there are also people who see no thoughts at all; their minds are completely blank. That is all right too. You are facing your own mind, so no one can judge you, and no one can grade your experience. Meditation is a completely personal experience; no two people’s experiences are exactly the same.

With continued practice, you will surely find that your experience sometimes changes from day to day, and sometimes one meditation differs from the next. At times you feel your thoughts are clear and easy to observe; at times they look blurry and indistinct, or slip away at once. Sometimes too, during formal meditation, you find your mind growing sluggish and dull. That is all right. This dullness is only a set of neurons commenting on your intention to meditate; you can simply observe the dullness or whatever other feeling you are experiencing.

Resting bare attention on the experience of the present moment is meditation. Even if a neuron arises with the thought “I don’t know how to meditate,” so long as you can watch it, it too can become a support for meditation.

So long as you maintain awareness, or mindfulness, no matter what happens in your practice, what you practice counts as meditation. Watching your thoughts is meditation; being unable to watch your thoughts is also meditation. These experiences can all be supports for meditation. The point is that whatever thoughts, emotions, or sensory perceptions arise, you maintain awareness. Whatever happens, you remember to maintain awareness—that is meditation. In this way, meditation becomes far easier than you ever imagined.
Whatever thought arises, do not try to block it.
—The Ninth Karmapa, The Ocean of Definitive Meaning (Mahamudra)

If you have only just begun to learn meditation, then simply watching the thoughts associated with unpleasant experiences may be very difficult—especially those connected with strong emotions such as jealousy, hatred, fear, or envy. These unpleasant thoughts are so tenacious that, before we know it, we become mired in them. I can’t count how many people have spoken to me about this problem, not with all my fingers and toes put together—especially after quarrels with family, colleagues, or others, when these unpleasant thoughts particularly refuse to let them go. Day after day they replay in their minds what they think they said or did, and find themselves sunk in a quagmire of thoughts, dwelling on how wicked the other person was, on what they could or should have said, or endlessly on how to get even.

The best way to face such thoughts is to step back and rest the mind for a minute in objectless calm-abiding meditation, and only then become aware of each thought, along with the many thoughts and ideas those thoughts give rise to. Observe the two directly for several minutes, just as you did in the meditation on form. Thus at times rest in objectless meditation, and at times alternately bring the attention back to those thoughts, practicing meditation with an object.

When you face negative thoughts in this way, two results arise. (Don’t worry, it has nothing to do with growing horns!) First, when you rest in awareness, your mind begins to settle; and second, you will find that your attention to these thoughts and storylines is itself coming and going, just as it did when you used sights, sounds, and other sensory perceptions as supports for meditation. When your thoughts are observed by an attention that is sometimes present and sometimes absent, just as thoughts can be interrupted by other things—like folding clothes, shopping, or preparing for a meeting—your thoughts are also interrupted by your awareness, and gradually these unpleasant thoughts’ grip on your mind slowly loosens. Then you begin to understand that these thoughts are not as solid and intense as they first appeared; they are more like a busy signal on the phone—perhaps annoying, but nothing you cannot handle.

When you use unpleasant thoughts in this way, they become an asset for settling the mind rather than a liability. It is also like going to the gym to lift weights, gradually increasing the load—except that you are training the muscles of the mind, and with time your capacity to handle stress grows stronger and stronger.
We need not feel we are wholly ruled by our emotions.
Kalu Rinpoche, Gentle Voices

Because emotions are mostly clear and persistent, they are more useful supports for meditation than thoughts. My father and my teachers taught me that emotions fall basically into three kinds: positive emotions, negative emotions, and neutral emotions.

Positive emotions, such as love, compassion, friendship, and loyalty, can strengthen our minds, nurture our confidence, and enhance our ability to help others. Some English translations of the Buddhist scriptures call these emotions and the related behaviors “
virtuous

”. At least from what I observe of Western audiences, such a rendering seems to carry some connection with morality. In fact, these behaviors and emotions have nothing at all to do with ethics or morality. One of my students, whose English is rather good, told me that the Tibetan word “
gewa
”, translated into English as “
virtue,”
is in fact closer to “
virtue”
’s earliest sense, which, in terms of healing, means “efficacious, effective.”

Negative emotions, such as fear, hatred, sadness, jealousy, grief, or envy, are usually translated as “unwholesome.” These emotions generally weaken our minds, undermine our confidence, and increase our sense of fear.

Then there are the neutral emotions. Neutral emotions are basically responses that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome—feelings neither positive nor negative, like the way we feel about a pencil, a sheet of paper, or a stapler. Just try it: it is no easy matter to feel either positive or negative about a pencil!

The way to use emotions as a support for meditation depends on the kind of emotion you are experiencing. If what you feel now is a positive, mind-strengthening emotion, then you can focus on that feeling and on its object. For example, if you feel love for a small child, you can place your attention on the child and on your love for that child. If you feel compassion for someone in difficulty, you can focus on the person who needs help and on your feeling of compassion. In this way the object of the emotion becomes a support for the emotion itself, and the emotion in turn also becomes a support that lets you focus on the object that inspired it.

By contrast, if we keep focusing on the object of a negative emotion, we usually strengthen within the mind the impression that the person, situation, or thing is “bad in itself.” However hard you try to bring forth compassion, faith, or other positive feelings, your mind will almost automatically produce this negative emotion toward that object: “Wow! That really is bad—you must get rid of it, fight it, or simply run away!”

When facing negative emotions, the more constructive approach is very much like meditating on negative thoughts: rest the attention on the emotion itself, not on its object. Just watch the emotion like this, without analyzing it in your head, without gripping the emotion, and without blocking it—simply observe it. When you do this, the emotion will not be as huge and intense as it first appeared.

In my first year of retreat, because I had suddenly to be with many people, fear and anxiety arose in me, and I felt driven to run back to my room to meditate alone. The method I used then was much like this. Once I began simply to observe my fears, I could see clearly that they were not solid and indissoluble monsters that I could never defeat. In fact, they were only a succession of tiny, fleeting physical sensations and impressions which, because they jumped in and out of awareness so quickly, looked as if they were solid and unified. (Later I also found that this is like a mass of rapidly spinning subatomic particles creating an appearance that seems indivisible and solid.) Having become aware of my fears in this way, I began to think: “Hmm, how amusing—the fear really is not that strong! In fact it is not even harmful—only a heap of fleeting sensations that appear, linger a second or two, and then vanish.”

Of course, this process did not happen overnight. It took me several weeks of immersing myself completely in it, like a passionate scientist buried in an experiment, and I was helped along by many years of training undergirding it.

From this experience I grew even more admiring of the many methods the Buddha taught centuries ago, for they were able to help people he had never even met to overcome all sorts of difficulties. As I began to learn more about the structure and function of the brain, and about the insights modern physicists have set forth on the nature of reality, I was truly astonished at the convergence between the meditation techniques the Buddha developed through introspection and the reasons scientists, through objective observation, have found to explain why those techniques work.

However, the objects associated with negative emotions—whether people, places, or events—are sometimes so clear and so deep that we truly cannot ignore their presence. When this happens, do not try to block them; rather, make good use of them, resting your attention on a sight, a smell, a taste, or whatever object you previously learned to use in meditation; then the object of the emotion itself can become a powerful support for meditation.

These methods are especially useful when you begin to confront directly the fundamental afflictions mentioned in the first part of this book. When I first studied the subject of afflictions, I thought: “How awful, I am full of faults, I am foolish, I have deep craving and hatred, and I shall suffer like this for the rest of my life.” Later, however, I heard an old saying, though I don’t know whether it is true or false, roughly to this effect: “The peacock eats a poisonous plant and uses its toxin to enhance the brilliance and splendor of its feathers.”
Because in childhood I had been cringing and huddled by fear and anxiety, I know very well the mighty power of the afflictions. For

years I felt every day that I was going to die, and to be freed from fear sometimes truly wished to be done with life quickly. Only when I went into retreat and was forced to face these afflictions directly did I learn that foolishness, craving, and hatred are in fact the very raw material of meditative practice, and like the poisonous grass the peacock eats, they are transformed into a wellspring of powerful blessing.

Every affliction is the foundation of wisdom. If we sink deeply into our afflictions, or try to repress them, we will in the end bind ourselves in our own cocoon and create still more problems for ourselves. But if we can turn and look directly at these afflictions, then those very things we dread will harm us gradually transform into the most powerful allies for meditation that we could hope for.
Afflictions are not our enemies; they are our friends.

This is a fact that is hard to accept, yet whenever you shrink back and cannot agree, think of the peacock. Poisonous plants are not to the palate’s liking, but should a peacock truly swallow them, it can turn that poison into its bright and splendid plumage.

In this final lesson of the practice, we have seen what meditative remedies one may apply when facing the most fearful and most painful experiences. Having examined these practices, we come to understand that every affliction which makes us retreat, take fright, or feel fragile holds an equal power to make us stronger, more confident, more open, and more able to receive the limitless possibilities of our own Buddha-nature.
